newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists challenge EU stability pact.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists challenge EU stability pact.

text.p: France's opposition Socialist party, challenging the fiscal orthodoxy underpinning European monetary union, said on Friday it wanted to review a stability pact meant to limit budget deficits after the launch of the new euro.

Party spokesman Francois Hollande told Reuters the Socialists opposed an assumption implicit in the pact that countries must continue to cut their budget deficits below three percent of gross domestic product after monetary union.
"We want to look at the stability pact again to get guarantees that we will not be obliged to go beyond three percent," he said.
"It is implicitly written in that we may have to go below three percent and go therefore towards an even more rigourous budgetary policy," he added.

The challenge to the pact, agreed last year after months of tough bargaining inside the EU, is the most controversial aspect of the Socialist party's policies on Europe, going right to the heart of a debate on the future shape of monetary union.

The Socialist party, which said it wanted growth and jobs in Europe rather than austerity and mass unemployment, also unveiled a manifesto for a parliamentary election on May 25 and June 1, in which it reaffirmed its commitment to the euro.
But it insisted it wanted Italy and Spain in at the start, along with Britain if it chose to do so.

And it said Maastricht treaty criteria must be interpreted flexibly, taking account of a provision in the treaty itself which suggests that a country could qualify for monetary union if it going in the right direction to meet these targets.

The party, which has been trailing in opinion polls, also called for a European economic government alongside the future European central bank, and said the euro must not be overvalued against the dollar or the yen.

Some of these conditions -- flexibility on Maastricht, and early Italian and Spanish membership -- have not been ruled out categorically by EU ministers who say such decisions must wait until the scheduled time in late April/early May 1998.
The Socialist party's insistence that the euro must not be overvalued has already been largely taken care of by the recent rise in the dollar.
And even the call for a European economic government is not too, too far away from an informal stability council backed by the EU to co-ordinate economic policies inside the euro zone.
But the challenge to the stability pact calls into question fundamental assumptions which have been made by EU countries as they stitch together the compromises needed to launch the euro.

Germany, distrusting its partners to follow its own tough stand on inflation and deficits, had insisted on the pact, which will commit monetary union members to tight fiscal policies by fining them if their deficits overshoot three percent of GDP.

To avoid such fines, the assumption is that EU countries would cut deficits to well below three percent -- possibly even to zero or to a surplus -- in good times, leaving them leeway to increase deficits to three percent in times of recession.
Hollande said the Socialists were against such new rigour.
"We must conduct a policy for growth, we need major public works, we must have a European social policy," he said.
To fund these public works, Dominique Strauss-Kahn, the party's spokesman on economic affairs, said that the reserves of central banks could be used to underwrite EU borrowings.

"Central bank reserves are proportional to imports. Given there will no longer be internal balances of payments once we have the euro, there will obviously be credit available, not for spending, but at least to use as a guarantee," he said.
Such an idea would likely be anathema to Germany, which made central bank independence a condition for signing up to the Maastricht treaty.

"The Socialists have adopted the idea that central bank reserves, which are the states' money, could be used for something other than the defending exchange rates, and it's probably not only Socialists who think these reserves could be used," said Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley in Paris.
